Ireland PoliticsHuge crowds turn out in support of residents over Drumcree parade disputeImage source, ReutersImage caption, Crowds have gathered at the Garvaghy Road to support local residents

Rallies are being held in Portadown on both sides of the Drumcree parade dispute as the stand-off between Garvaghy Road residents and the Orange Order continues.

It comes after the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said a "major public safety operation" will continue in Portadown this weekend.

Speaking to thousands at an event on the Garvaghy Road, First Minister and Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O'Neill said she heard the Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant "talk about being between a rock and a hard place", adding she has "never heard such nonsense, this is between right and wrong".

Speaking at Drumcree church, Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart repeated calls for PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher and his officers to "do their job" and facilitate the parade, describing the current impasse as "mob rule".

The fallout over the proposed march - which is opposed by residents of the Garvaghy Road - has lasted since Sunday morning.

Huge crowds have turned up on the Garvaghy Road on Saturday to support local residents.

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

Published4 days agoAn uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded

Published11 hours agoO'Neill said that "if this British government isn't prepared to end this crisis, then it's up to the thousands here, to collectively stand with the Garvaghy Road residents".

She said: "We will stand shoulder to shoulder for as long as it takes."

Former SDLP MLA Dolores Kelly said: "Never again did we think we'd be on the Garvaghy Road again to say no going back and no Orange Order parades in the Garvaghy Road."

A smaller event is being held in the Edgarstown area in Portadown in support of the Orange Order.

Image caption, An event is being held in the Edgarstown area in Portadown in support of the Orange Order

Speaking to BBC News NI at Drumcree, Lockhart said there could be "repercussions for a very long time if mob rule wins over the rule of law".

Asked if we had stepped back from the "abyss" cited by both Lockhart and a High Court Judge in reference to last week's court proceedings, Lockhart was firm that no progress had yet been made.

"No, we need the police service to step up and do their job. I do think if the real residents step forward we can and should discuss further options and resolutions, because we do want to see this resolved," Lockhart said.

"Where I see the abyss is for the PSNI. It needs community and political support and if they allow mob rule to win in NI, I think we are staring down the abyss in terms of confidence in the rule of law."

Image caption, Liam McDonald said people did not want to see any more "trouble or strife"

Liam McDonald travelled from south Armagh and said it was important for him to be at the Garvaghy Road.

"The majority of people in Ireland, right across the island, don't want any more of this. They don't want to see any more trouble or strife or anything like that.

"How they're going to solve this, I would love to know the answer, but I don't. And I think a lot of people are in the same boat. They don't know what the answer is to it. But it has to be solved."

Image caption, Noah Bell was born after the Good Friday Agreement and described himself as part of the "peace process generation"

Noah Bell attended the Edgarstown event in support of the Portadown District and said he believed the situation was "really worrying" and wanted the parade to be allowed to proceed.

"I'm part of the so-called peace process generation. I was born after the Good Friday Agreement. But I've been aware about the stories of years gone by.

"I think the determination should be upheld. The law's on our side and that lawful determination must be upheld and the parade allowed to go through."

Image caption, Francis McGowan recalled "really frightening" times during previous disputes

Francis McGowan said she wanted to show her support for people on the Garvaghy Road and did not want to see a return to the past.

"I remember back, it was awful times. Really frightening things as well, so we do not want to return under any circumstances.

"Especially for the younger generation, we don't want to go back through the dark, dark days. So I think it's important that way to speak of them."

Image caption, Jonathan Jackson described himself as a young Protestant unionist and a first-generation Orangeman.

Jonathan Jackson, who is a member of the Orange Order, said he at the Edgarstown rally because he believed in his culture and was proud of his identity.

"For me, as a young Protestant Unionist, it does begin to feel like a cold house for me in my own country.

"So I think obviously you can look back and maybe seems like an older person's issue, but I do think this is a civil liberties issue."

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant said he was "concerned at the prolonged standoff" which he said was "ultimately in nobody's interests".

"I have been working with all those involved to find a mutually acceptable solution," he said in a social media post, external on Saturday.

He said he was grateful to those engaging in dialogue, adding that it was "a crucial time" for Northern Ireland and he hoped compromise could be found.

"Leadership is never easy at moments like this but I commend all those who are trying to get to a solution."

A spokesperson for Fianna Fáil said the taoiseach believes "now is a time for us to be calm and careful in what we say", adding there is a "history of hurt around Drumcree".

They said: "While no agreement has been reached, it is crucial that channels of communication remain open."

Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said the PSNI is doing everything it can to maintain order and ensure the safety of everyone in that area

The PSNI said it was "continuing to seek safe and peaceful compliance" with the Parades Commission's decision that the Orange Order parade could go ahead with restrictions.

On Wednesday, the PSNI Chief Constable said there would be an investigation after protesters blocked the mainly nationalist road to prevent the parade from happening.

Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said on Friday that the "investigation into anyone suspected of breaking the law related to this dispute is continuing at pace".

He added that the PSNI are doing "everything we can to maintain order and ensure the safety of everyone" in Portadown.
